headline: Indigenous Forests Strike Gold with New Conservation Market
meta_description: Four Indigenous communities in Panama's Darién forest are documenting wildlife to earn revenue through biodiversity credits, protecting threatened lands.
summary_short: Indigenous villages in Panama's Darién forest are turning forest conservation into income by documenting over 200 species and joining the biodiversity credit market.
body:
Four Indigenous Wounaan and Emberá-Wounaan villages in Panama's Darién forest have found a novel way to protect their threatened lands: they've launched a biodiversity monitoring project that transforms conservation data into market value. Working across 18,000 hectares of forest, the communities documented more than 200 species, including jaguars, Baird's tapirs, and crested eagles—three "umbrella" species that indicate broader ecosystem health. At least 15 of the recorded species face threats from extinction. Now the communities plan to use this baseline data to enter the biodiversity credit market, hoping to generate much-needed revenue in a region where economic opportunities remain scarce.

The project combines modern technology with Indigenous stewardship. Working alongside Panama-based FSC Indigenous Foundation and the international nonprofit Health In Harmony, community members employ bioacoustic monitoring and camera-trapping techniques developed by Savimbo, a biodiversity credit company co-founded by Indigenous members themselves. The methodology tracks 15 indicator species to measure forest health.

Perhaps most striking is the immediate cultural shift the effort has sparked. Samuel Cheucarama, a resident of one Wounaan village, witnessed his neighbors transforming their relationship with the forest. "People don't go hunting anymore," he observed. "They're saying, 'We're going to put up a 'No Hunting' sign." What began as a data-gathering initiative has become something deeper—a community-wide commitment to conservation, driven by locals recognizing both the ecological and economic value of their forests. As illegal logging and agricultural expansion threaten the Darién, these villages are proving that Indigenous knowledge and modern markets can align to protect some of Earth's most biodiverse places.
quick_facts: Four Wounaan and Emberá-Wounaan villages in Panama's Darién forest
Documented over 200 species across 18,000 hectares of threatened forest
Using biodiversity credits to generate revenue for conservation
Three umbrella species: jaguars, tapirs, and crested eagles
Community behavior shifted—residents now support hunting restrictions
